challenges.intro_fact: Spring is here — and so is a good moment to ask: what small changes can stick? Ireland produces 4x more food than it eats, but also generates over 1 million tonnes of food waste a year. The biggest changes often start in the kitchen.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture?
questions.fact: Agriculture accounts for about 35% of Ireland's total emissions — one of the highest shares in Europe. Most of that comes from livestock, particularly cattle.

questions.text: Which everyday action has the single biggest impact on an individual's carbon footprint?
questions.fact: Cutting out one long-haul flight saves more CO₂ than a year of recycling. Transport — especially aviation — is one of the highest-impact areas for individual action.

questions.text: Research shows that habits form fastest when they are tied to what?
questions.fact: Habit stacking — linking a new behaviour to an existing routine — is one of the most effective techniques in behaviour change research.

challenges.action_intro: Spring is a natural reset point. Small changes compounded over weeks add up — and April is a great month to start. Pick one or two things you can genuinely stick to.

actions.title: Pick one sustainable habit to add this week
actions.desc: Choose something small and specific — like bringing a bag to the shops or switching off standby devices before bed. Attach it to something you already do every day.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute home energy audit
actions.desc: Walk around your home and note anything that uses energy unnecessarily — old bulbs, devices on standby, gaps in doors or windows. Most fixes take minutes.
actions.carbon: Up to 100 kg CO₂/year if acted on

actions.title: Plan one meat-free day per week for April
actions.desc: Commit to one full day each week without meat for the month. That alone could save around 50–100 kg CO₂ over the month.

challenges.intro_fact: April Fools' Day — so let's sort the facts from the fiction. Only 16% of Irish people think they personally need to do more on climate, yet 72% of global emissions trace back to household behaviour. Some of the biggest climate myths are the most widely believed.

questions.text: True or false: recycling is the most impactful thing an individual can do for the climate.
options: True — recycling is the top action
False — diet change has far more impact
False — switching energy provider is bigger
True — plastic is the main issue
questions.fact: Recycling is important but relatively low impact compared to diet, transport and home heating. Shifting to a plant-rich diet can save 10x more CO₂ per year than optimising your recycling.

questions.text: Which of these has the LOWEST carbon footprint?
questions.fact: Oat milk has the lowest overall footprint when you combine carbon, land and water use. It produces about 80% less CO₂ than cow's milk and uses far less water than almond milk.

questions.text: Electric cars produce zero emissions. True or false?
options: False — they run on coal in Ireland
True — once the battery is made
questions.fact: Manufacturing an EV creates roughly 8 tonnes of CO₂ — mostly from the battery. But over its lifetime an EV still produces far less than a petrol car.

challenges.action_intro: Climate myths are everywhere — and even well-meaning people believe them. Understanding what actually matters is the first step to making changes that count.

actions.title: Check one climate 'fact' you believe and verify it
actions.desc: Pick something you think you know about climate and look it up on Our World in Data or the EPA Ireland site. You might be surprised.

actions.title: Share one surprising fact with someone today
actions.desc: Pick the most surprising thing you learned in this quiz and mention it to one person. Research shows peer conversations are more effective than media campaigns at shifting views.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Autism Awareness Day. Research consistently shows that time in nature improves wellbeing for everyone — reducing stress, improving focus and lifting mood. Yet access to green space in Ireland is very unequal depending on where you live.

questions.text: How much time in nature per week is linked to significantly better wellbeing, according to research?
questions.fact: A large UK study found that spending at least 2 hours per week in nature is linked to significantly better health and wellbeing — even spread across multiple short visits.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people live within 15 minutes walk of a public green space?
questions.fact: Around 70% of Irish people live within a 15-minute walk of a public park or green space — but that drops in some suburban and rural areas without proper footpaths.

questions.text: Which Irish initiative aims to increase biodiversity by letting parts of public parks grow wild?
questions.fact: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan encourages councils, farmers and households to let grass grow longer, plant wildflowers and reduce pesticide use. Over 1,000 organisations have signed up.

challenges.action_intro: Access to green space isn't just nice to have — it is a public health issue. Small actions across thousands of gardens genuinely add up for biodiversity.

actions.title: Spend 30 minutes outside in a green space this week
actions.desc: It doesn't have to be wild — a local park counts. Leave the headphones behind if you can and just notice what's around you.

actions.title: Let a patch of your garden or windowsill go wild
actions.desc: Stop cutting one corner of the lawn, or plant a small pot of wildflowers on your windowsill. Even tiny wild patches support pollinators in urban areas.

challenges.intro_fact: Good Friday in Ireland has traditionally meant fish instead of meat. Ireland has one of Europe's largest exclusive economic zones, yet imports most of its seafood while exporting much of what it catches.

questions.text: What percentage of the world's fish stocks are currently overfished or fished at maximum capacity?
questions.fact: Over 90% of global fish stocks are now fully or over-exploited, according to the FAO. That's up from 10% in the 1970s — a dramatic shift in just 50 years.

questions.text: Which of these fish is considered a more sustainable choice in Irish waters?
questions.fact: Mackerel is one of the more sustainable choices in Irish waters — it's abundant, low in the food chain and caught without destructive methods.

questions.text: How much CO₂ does a portion of farmed salmon produce compared to a portion of chicken?
questions.fact: Farmed salmon produces roughly twice the CO₂ of chicken per kg — mainly because of the energy-intensive feed. Wild-caught small fish like mackerel or sardines are far lower.

challenges.action_intro: The sea gives Ireland a lot — coastline, food, tourism and identity. Looking after it starts with what we put on our plates.

actions.title: Check the sustainability rating of your fish today
actions.desc: The Good Fish Guide by the Marine Conservation Society rates fish by sustainability. Check goodfishguide.org before you buy fish this week.

actions.title: Try mackerel, mussels or sardines this week
actions.desc: These are among the most sustainable and nutritious seafood options in Ireland — and usually cheaper than salmon or tuna. Tinned works just as well.

challenges.intro_fact: April is when Ireland comes alive. Over 11,000 species of plants and animals are found in Ireland — and spring is the busiest season for most of them. But biodiversity has declined significantly over the past 50 years, largely due to changes in farming.

questions.text: What proportion of Ireland's land is covered by peatland (bog)?
questions.fact: About 20% of Ireland's land area is peatland — one of the highest proportions in Europe. Intact bogs store enormous amounts of carbon but have been heavily damaged by drainage and peat cutting.

questions.text: Which Irish habitat has seen the steepest decline in recent decades?
questions.fact: Raised bogs have lost over 90% of their natural condition in Ireland. They are slow to form — some are 10,000 years old — and almost impossible to fully restore once drained.

questions.text: How many species of wild bee are found in Ireland?
questions.fact: Ireland has around 100 species of wild bee, including 20 bumblebee species. One third of these are threatened with extinction — mainly due to loss of flower-rich habitats and pesticide use.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's biodiversity is genuinely special — but it is under pressure. The good news is that gardens, balconies and even window boxes can play a real role.

actions.title: Download the iNaturalist app and log one species this week
actions.desc: iNaturalist is free and lets you photograph plants, birds or insects and have them identified automatically. Every observation contributes to national biodiversity data.

actions.title: Plant one native Irish wildflower this spring
actions.desc: Primrose, cowslip, wild garlic or ox-eye daisy are all easy to grow in pots or gardens and support native insects. Most garden centres stock them from April.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland gets plenty of rain — but that doesn't mean we're off the hook on water. The average Irish person uses about 150 litres of water per day at home, but their total water footprint including food and products is closer to 4,000 litres a day.

questions.text: How many litres of water does it take to produce 1 kg of beef?
questions.fact: 1 kg of beef requires roughly 15,000 litres of water — most of it for growing the feed crops. That's about 100 showers worth for a single kilo of meat.

questions.text: Which product uses more water to produce — a cotton T-shirt or a litre of wine?
options: A litre of wine uses more
questions.fact: A cotton T-shirt takes about 2,700 litres of water to produce — equivalent to roughly 3 years of drinking water for one person.

questions.text: What is the main water-related environmental problem facing Irish rivers right now?
questions.fact: Agricultural runoff — carrying excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers and slurry — is the leading cause of poor water quality in Irish rivers. Only 53% of Irish water bodies are in good ecological status.

challenges.action_intro: Water is easy to take for granted in Ireland — but the water embedded in our food and clothes is a global issue. Farmers in water-stressed regions grow the crops that end up on our plates.

actions.title: Fix a dripping tap at home this week
actions.desc: A dripping tap wastes up to 15 litres a day — that's over 5,000 litres a year. Most fixes take 10 minutes and cost very little.

actions.title: Eat one less portion of beef this week
actions.desc: Replacing one beef meal with chicken, fish or legumes saves not just carbon but a significant amount of embedded water.

challenges.intro_fact: April is one of the best months to spot Ireland's wildflowers. Hedgerows are one of Ireland's most important habitats, home to over 80% of our mammal species, most of our breeding birds, and thousands of insects.

questions.text: How many kilometres of hedgerow does Ireland have?
questions.fact: Ireland has approximately 700,000 km of hedgerows — more per square kilometre than almost any other country in Europe. They are a uniquely Irish habitat and a vital carbon store.

questions.text: What is the main threat to Irish hedgerows right now?
questions.fact: Agricultural removal and mechanical cutting — often outside the legal cutting season — are the main threats. It's illegal to cut hedges between 1 March and 31 August to protect nesting birds.

questions.text: Which common Irish wildflower is one of the best early-season food sources for bees?
questions.fact: Gorse (furze) flowers almost year-round and is one of the most important early nectar sources for bumblebees in Ireland. There's an old Irish saying: 'When gorse is out of bloom, kissing is out of season.'

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's wild landscape is shaped by its hedgerows, bogs and coastal habitats. Getting to know them is the first step to caring about them.

actions.title: Go for a hedgerow walk and identify 3 species
actions.desc: Use the free iNaturalist or PlantNet app to identify what's growing in a local hedgerow. Hawthorn, blackthorn and elder are the most common in Ireland.

actions.title: Plant a native Irish hedgerow plant in your garden
actions.desc: Hawthorn, blackthorn or hazel are all cheap, fast-growing and excellent for wildlife. Even a single plant in a garden makes a difference for birds and insects.

challenges.intro_fact: In Ireland, 1 in 4 people will experience a mental health difficulty at some point. Yet one of the most effective interventions is also the most underused: spending time in nature. The science behind 'green prescribing' is growing fast.

questions.text: By how much can a 90-minute walk in nature reduce activity in the brain area linked to negative thinking?
questions.fact: Stanford researchers found that a 90-minute walk in nature significantly reduced neural activity in the prefrontal cortex — the area linked to rumination and anxiety.

questions.text: What is 'green prescribing' as used in Irish healthcare?
options: GPs recommending nature-based activities instead of or alongside medication
A government scheme to plant trees near hospitals
questions.fact: Green prescribing involves GPs recommending nature-based activities — walking, gardening, birdwatching — as part of treatment for anxiety, depression and loneliness. It is growing across Irish primary care.

questions.text: Which Irish programme connects people with mental health difficulties to outdoor nature activities?
questions.fact: Green Care Ireland connects people experiencing mental health and social difficulties with therapeutic nature-based activities — farming, gardening, animal care and conservation work.

challenges.action_intro: Mental health and the environment are deeply connected. When we look after nature, it looks after us — and the evidence for this is stronger than ever.

actions.title: Take a 20-minute walk outside without your phone this week
actions.desc: Leave the podcast and headphones behind just once. Walk somewhere green if you can — a park, a canal path, a beach. Notice what you see, hear and smell.

actions.title: Suggest a walking meeting at work this week
actions.desc: Replace one sit-down meeting with a walk-and-talk outside. It's better for creativity, better for wellbeing, and uses no energy.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the most vibrant live music scenes in the world. A single large music festival can produce over 500 tonnes of CO₂ — mainly from travel, generators and single-use waste. More festivals are now trying to change that.

questions.text: What proportion of a typical music festival's carbon footprint comes from audience travel?
questions.fact: Up to 80% of a festival's total carbon footprint comes from how the audience gets there. Encouraging public transport, carpooling and cycling can make a huge difference.

questions.text: Which Irish festival was among the first in Europe to introduce a reusable cup system?
questions.fact: Electric Picnic introduced a reusable cup system early on. Body & Soul has also been a pioneer — running on 100% renewable energy.

questions.text: How much waste does the average festival-goer generate per day?
questions.fact: Festival-goers generate around 3 kg of waste per day — roughly 3x the daily average at home. Much of that is avoidable: food packaging, single-use cups, and abandoned tents.

challenges.action_intro: Festivals are one of the great joys of Irish summer — and the industry is changing fast. Our choices around travel and waste are the two biggest levers we have.

actions.title: If you're going to a festival this summer, plan to travel by public transport
actions.desc: Most major Irish festivals are served by shuttle buses or trains. Check the transport options now and book early — it's usually cheaper and takes the parking stress away.
actions.carbon: Could save 20–50 kg CO₂ vs driving alone

actions.title: Pack a festival kit that cuts waste
actions.desc: Reusable cup, water bottle, solid shampoo bar, and a bag for sorting recycling. Most of this costs nothing if you already have it.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland has one of the richest marine environments in Europe. The Shannon Estuary has one of the only resident bottlenose dolphin populations in Europe, and Irish waters are home to over 25 species of whales and dolphins.

questions.text: What percentage of the world's oxygen is produced by ocean phytoplankton?
questions.fact: About 50% of the world's oxygen is produced by marine phytoplankton. The ocean also absorbs around 25% of our CO₂ emissions each year, making it our biggest climate ally.

questions.text: What is the main threat to the Shannon Estuary dolphins today?
options: Boat disturbance, pollution and fishing bycatch
questions.fact: The Shannon dolphins face multiple threats: boat disturbance, marine pollution, and accidental capture in fishing nets (bycatch). The population of around 115 animals is considered vulnerable.

questions.text: How much plastic enters the world's oceans every year?
questions.fact: Around 8 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year — equivalent to a rubbish truck emptying into the sea every minute.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's ocean is one of our greatest natural assets — and it is under real pressure from plastic, pollution and climate change. What we do on land ends up in the sea.

actions.title: Take part in a Clean Coasts beach clean this month
actions.desc: Clean Coasts Ireland runs regular community beach cleans around the whole coast. Find one at cleancoasts.org — they provide bags and gloves.

actions.title: Switch to a plastic-free shampoo or soap bar
actions.desc: Shampoo bars last 2–3x longer than bottled versions and avoid the plastic entirely. Several Irish brands now make them.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Art Day. Climate grief, hope and action are increasingly central themes in Irish art — from theatre to visual art to music. Can culture change minds where facts can't?

questions.text: Research on climate communication suggests which approach is most effective at motivating behaviour change?
options: Stories of real people making positive change
questions.fact: Narrative and personal stories are consistently more effective than data or fear-based messaging at motivating action. People connect with people — not with statistics.

questions.text: What is 'solastalgia' — a term increasingly used in climate discussions?
options: Grief for environmental changes in one's home place
The mental health benefit of nature
questions.fact: Solastalgia describes the emotional distress caused by environmental change in one's home environment. It's increasingly recognised in Irish farming and coastal communities facing climate change.

questions.text: Which of these describes the relationship between Irish culture and the natural world?
options: Largely separate — Irish culture is urban
Historically close — land, bog and coast run through Irish writing and art
Only recently connected through climate activism
questions.fact: Land, bog, coast and seasons run through Irish writing and art — from Seamus Heaney's bogs to contemporary climate artists. Nature and Irish cultural identity have always been closely intertwined.

challenges.action_intro: Facts inform. Stories move people to act. That's why art, games, music and storytelling are not extras in the climate conversation — they are central to it.

actions.title: Find one piece of art, music or writing about nature or climate this week
actions.desc: A poem, a documentary, an album, a painting — it doesn't matter. Notice how it makes you feel. Art reaches the parts that facts sometimes can't.
actions.carbon: Builds emotional connection to the issue

actions.title: Support an Irish environmental arts project
actions.desc: Look up Commonage, Phizzfest or similar Irish environmental arts programmes. Even sharing their work on social media helps build the audience for climate culture.

challenges.intro_fact: 42% of Irish people say they feel lectured when climate topics come up — and that stops the conversation before it starts. Learning to talk about climate in a way that connects rather than alienates is one of the most useful skills you can develop.

questions.text: According to research, what is the most effective opening for a climate conversation?
options: Ask what they care about and connect it to climate
Tell them what changes they need to make
questions.fact: Starting with shared values — not climate facts — is the most effective approach. If someone cares about their children's health, or their local landscape, those are the doors into the conversation.

questions.text: What percentage of people globally are worried about climate change but rarely discuss it?
questions.fact: Research by Yale found that around 60–65% of people are worried about climate change but rarely talk about it — creating a 'spiral of silence' where everyone thinks they are in the minority.

questions.text: The '25% tipping point' theory suggests social norms shift when what proportion of a community commits to a new behaviour?
questions.fact: Research backed by the IPCC shows just 10–25% of committed individuals can shift a social norm for the whole group. You don't need everyone — just enough people willing to act visibly.

challenges.action_intro: Most people want to do more — they just don't know how to start. Talking openly and without judgement is one of the most powerful things any of us can do.

actions.title: Have one climate conversation this week — without lecturing
actions.desc: Start by asking someone what they think about something local — the weather, food prices, a nature story in the news. Listen first. Share one surprising fact if it feels natural.

actions.title: Share one thing you learned today on social media or WhatsApp
actions.desc: Even a short message or forwarding this quiz to one person breaks the spiral of silence. You don't need to be an expert — just curious.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Creativity and Innovation Day. Ireland has quietly become a hub for clean tech — from offshore wind potential to green hydrogen research. Ireland has enough offshore wind resource to power the country several times over.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in 2024?
questions.fact: In 2024, around 60% of Ireland's electricity came from renewables — mainly wind power. Ireland's target is 80% by 2030, one of the more ambitious in Europe.

questions.text: Ireland's offshore wind resource is estimated to be how many times larger than its current electricity demand?
questions.fact: Ireland's offshore wind resource has been estimated at more than 10 times its current electricity demand — potentially making Ireland a major exporter of clean energy to Europe.

questions.text: What is 'green hydrogen' and why is it relevant to Ireland?
options: Hydrogen made using excess wind energy — Ireland has several projects underway
A government grant for home heating
A new type of solar panel technology
questions.fact: Green hydrogen is made by using surplus wind electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Ireland's windy west coast makes it well placed to produce green hydrogen for export to Europe.

challenges.action_intro: Ireland's clean energy story is one of the most exciting in Europe — and the transition creates jobs, cuts bills and reduces our dependence on imported fossil fuels.

actions.title: Check if your home energy provider offers a green tariff
actions.desc: Many Irish energy suppliers now offer tariffs where your electricity is matched to renewable generation. Switching can take less than 10 minutes online.

actions.title: Look into the SEAI home retrofit grant scheme
actions.desc: The SEAI offers grants of up to €25,000 for home insulation, heat pumps and solar panels. Even reading through the options at seai.ie is a useful first step.
actions.carbon: Potential to cut home emissions by 50–70%

challenges.intro_fact: Earth Day is celebrated every year on 22 April by over 1 billion people in 193 countries. It was first held in 1970 and led directly to the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people say they are willing to make some changes to address climate change?
questions.fact: 80% of Irish people say they are willing to make some changes — but only 16% believe they personally should be doing more. That gap is the challenge Environmentle is designed to help close.

questions.text: What share of total greenhouse gas emissions worldwide is linked to household behaviour?
questions.fact: 72% of all global greenhouse gas emissions can be traced back to household consumption — energy, food, transport and goods. Individual choices, multiplied across millions, are not small.

questions.text: Research suggests that once what proportion of a population commits to a new norm, it can spread to the rest?
questions.fact: The 25% Revolution, backed by IPCC research, shows that shifting a social norm only requires 10–25% of individuals to be deeply committed. Your actions influence the people around you.

challenges.action_intro: Earth Day is a moment to reflect and act. Small individual actions, multiplied across millions of people, genuinely add up. You don't need to fix everything — just do your bit.

actions.title: Calculate your carbon footprint today
actions.desc: Use a free online calculator — try myclimate.org or the WWF footprint calculator. It takes 5 minutes and shows where your biggest impact areas are.

actions.title: Commit to one meat-free day per week
actions.desc: Switching one day per week from meat to plant-based food is one of the highest-impact individual diet changes. Try it for April first.

actions.title: Talk to 3 people about climate action this week
actions.desc: Share what you learned today. Research shows social norms shift when people talk openly about behaviour change — and most people are more open than you'd expect.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is UNESCO World Book Day. Reading is one of the most effective ways to shift perspective — and the quality of climate writing has never been better. From hopeful rewilding books to page-turning climate science, there is something for everyone.

questions.text: Which book ranked reducing food waste and a plant-rich diet higher than solar panels as climate solutions?
options: This Changes Everything by Naomi Klein
The Sixth Extinction by Elizabeth Kolbert
questions.fact: 'Drawdown' edited by Paul Hawken ranked the top 100 solutions to climate change by impact. Reducing food waste and a plant-rich diet ranked higher than solar panels — genuinely surprising.

questions.text: What does research say about people who read fiction about climate change?
options: They become more anxious and less likely to act
They show increased empathy and willingness to act
It has no measurable effect on attitudes
They focus on fictional solutions, not real ones
questions.fact: Studies show that reading climate fiction increases empathy for those affected and raises the likelihood of pro-environmental behaviour. Stories build the emotional connection that facts alone cannot.

questions.text: Which Irish or Ireland-connected writer is known for engaging with themes of nature, land and bog?
questions.fact: Seamus Heaney's poetry is deeply rooted in the Irish bogland and rural landscape — his work helped generations connect with the natural world and understand land as something precious and fragile.

challenges.action_intro: Understanding is the foundation of action — and there has never been more good reading, listening and watching available on climate and nature.

actions.title: Add one climate or nature book to your reading list
actions.desc: Try 'Braiding Sweetgrass' by Robin Wall Kimmerer, 'Feral' by George Monbiot, or 'How to Avoid a Climate Disaster' by Bill Gates. Your local library will likely have at least one.

actions.title: Listen to one episode of a climate or nature podcast this week
actions.desc: Try 'How to Save a Planet', 'Outrage + Optimism', or 'The Irish Times Climate Podcast'. Even one episode can shift how you think about the issue.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland is one of the least forested countries in Europe — only about 11% of land is covered by trees, compared to an EU average of 38%. Most of that is commercial Sitka spruce. But native woodland is slowly recovering.

questions.text: What percentage of Ireland's land area is covered by native woodland?
questions.fact: Less than 1% of Ireland is covered by native woodland — one of the lowest in Europe. Once Ireland was covered in oak, ash and hazel. Most was cleared for farming and fuel over thousands of years.

questions.text: How much CO₂ can a single mature oak tree absorb per year?
questions.fact: A mature oak tree absorbs roughly 22 kg of CO₂ per year. The real carbon value of forests comes from the soil beneath them, which can store 3–5x more carbon than the trees themselves.

questions.text: What is Ireland's current target for forest cover by 2050?
questions.fact: Ireland's target is 18% forest cover by 2050 — still below the EU average, but a significant increase from today. Meeting it requires planting around 8,000 hectares per year, which Ireland is currently short of.

challenges.action_intro: Planting trees is not a silver bullet for climate change — but native woodland restoration is genuinely important for carbon, biodiversity and water quality in Ireland. Every tree helps.

actions.title: Plant a tree — or fund one being planted
actions.desc: Native Irish trees like oak, birch, hazel or rowan. If you don't have a garden, organisations like Easy Treesie or Native Woodland Trust plant on your behalf.

actions.title: Choose wood products with FSC certification
actions.desc: The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) label means timber came from responsibly managed forests. Look for it on paper, furniture and wood products — widely available in Irish shops.

challenges.intro_fact: Ireland generates about 14 million tonnes of waste every year — one of the highest per-capita rates in Europe. Most of that is avoidable. The circular economy is about designing waste out from the start.

questions.text: What percentage of materials that enter the global economy are still in use 6 months after purchase?
questions.fact: The Ellen MacArthur Foundation found that only about 9% of materials that enter the global economy are still in productive use 6 months later. The rest ends up in landfill, incineration or stockpiles.

questions.text: Which of these is the most effective waste reduction strategy according to the waste hierarchy?
questions.fact: The waste hierarchy puts refusal and reduction at the top — the best waste is waste that was never created. Recycling is near the bottom; it still uses energy and creates emissions.

questions.text: What does the EU Right to Repair directive require from manufacturers?
options: All products must come with a 10-year warranty
Manufacturers must provide spare parts and repair services for common products
All electronics must be repairable by the consumer
Products must be made from 50% recycled materials
questions.fact: The EU Right to Repair directive requires manufacturers of certain products — white goods, electronics, smartphones — to provide spare parts, repair manuals and repair services for a set number of years after sale.

challenges.action_intro: The most sustainable product is the one you already own. Before buying anything new this week, ask: can I borrow it, repair it, or buy it second-hand?

actions.title: Repair something instead of replacing it this week
actions.desc: A torn bag, a broken button, a cracked phone case — look up a repair tutorial before buying a replacement. Repair Cafés operate in most Irish cities and are free to attend.
actions.carbon: Extends product life, avoids manufacturing emissions

actions.title: Declutter one drawer or shelf and donate or sell what you don't use
actions.desc: Donating to charity shops, selling on Done Deal or giving away on Buy Nothing groups keeps items in circulation and out of landfill.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is World Day for Safety and Health at Work. Burnout costs Irish businesses an estimated €1.5 billion per year in lost productivity. Workplaces with stronger sustainability cultures tend to have higher employee wellbeing and lower turnover.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish workers say they would prefer to work for a company with strong environmental values?
questions.fact: Surveys consistently show around 65–70% of workers — rising to over 80% among under-35s — prefer to work for companies with genuine sustainability commitments.

questions.text: Which workplace intervention has the strongest evidence for improving employee wellbeing?
options: Access to natural light and greenery
questions.fact: Access to natural light and indoor plants consistently ranks among the strongest predictors of workplace wellbeing — yet most Irish office environments still underinvest in it.

questions.text: What does 'scope 3 emissions' mean in a workplace context?
options: Emissions from employee commuting and the supply chain
Emissions outside a company's legal obligation
questions.fact: Scope 3 emissions cover indirect emissions — including employee commuting, business travel, and the supply chain. For most Irish businesses, these represent 70–90% of their total carbon footprint.

challenges.action_intro: Workplace sustainability and employee wellbeing go hand in hand — and Irish businesses are starting to take both seriously. You don't need to be the CEO to start a conversation about it.

actions.title: Suggest one green initiative at your workplace this week
actions.desc: It could be as simple as asking about switching to a green energy tariff, starting a composting scheme, or setting up a lunchtime walking group.

actions.title: Swap one car commute for walking, cycling or public transport
actions.desc: Even one day per week makes a difference. Most Irish cities now have Bike to Work schemes and Leap card subsidies through employers.

challenges.intro_fact: Today is Stop Food Waste Day. Irish households throw away an estimated €700 worth of food every year — that's about €60 a month per family. Food waste in Ireland produces around 1.6 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually. Most of it is completely avoidable.

questions.text: What percentage of all food produced globally is wasted?
questions.fact: Roughly one third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted. If food waste were a country, it would be the third largest emitter of greenhouse gases in the world.

questions.text: Which food category is most wasted in Irish homes?
questions.fact: Fresh fruit and vegetables are the most wasted food category in Irish homes, followed by bread. Most happens because people buy more than they need or don't use produce before it goes off.

questions.text: According to Project Drawdown, reducing food waste is ranked how among all climate solutions?
questions.fact: Reducing food waste ranks in the top 5 climate solutions globally according to Project Drawdown — higher than solar panels, electric vehicles or wind power.

challenges.action_intro: Wasting less food is one of the single highest-impact climate actions you can take — and it saves you money at the same time. A weekly meal plan and a fridge check before shopping are all it takes to start.

actions.title: Do a fridge audit before your next food shop
actions.desc: Before you go shopping this week, check what's already in your fridge and cupboards. Write a list based on what you actually need. Stick to it.

actions.title: Try one 'use it up' meal this week
actions.desc: Cook one meal entirely from what's already in the fridge and cupboards — no new shopping. It's often surprisingly good and saves money and waste.

actions.title: Download the Too Good To Go app
actions.desc: Too Good To Go lets you buy surplus food from local restaurants, cafés and supermarkets at a fraction of the price. Available in Dublin, Cork, Galway and many other Irish towns.

challenges.intro_fact: We talk a lot about carbon and plastic — but pollution comes in many forms. Noise pollution, light pollution and air quality are all significant environmental health issues in Irish cities, and all are linked to climate-related choices like transport and energy.

questions.text: According to the WHO, noise pollution is the second largest environmental health risk in Europe after what?
questions.fact: The WHO identifies noise pollution as the second largest environmental health risk in Europe after air pollution, linked to cardiovascular disease, sleep disruption and cognitive impairment.

questions.text: What percentage of Irish people are exposed to road traffic noise above EU recommended levels?
questions.fact: Around 30% of Irish people are exposed to road traffic noise above EU recommended levels — with the highest exposure in Dublin, Cork and Limerick city centres.

questions.text: How did reduced car traffic during COVID-19 lockdowns affect bird biodiversity in cities?
options: Slightly negative — birds use road noise as navigation
Significantly positive — more species and more complex birdsong
Mixed results depending on the city
questions.fact: Studies found that reducing traffic noise led to significantly richer birdsong — more species, more complex songs, and birds able to communicate over longer distances.

challenges.action_intro: Pollution isn't always visible. Noise, light and air quality all affect our health and the health of wildlife around us — and many of the fixes are the same: fewer cars, more green space, cleaner energy.

actions.title: Create a quiet hour at home this evening — no screens, no background noise
actions.desc: Turn off the TV and music for one hour. Read, cook, chat or sit outside. Notice how your body responds to the quiet.

actions.title: Walk or cycle instead of driving for one short trip this week
actions.desc: Every car journey replaced by walking or cycling removes noise, reduces air pollution, cuts carbon and is good for your health.
